title: Why memories need their own test
summary: Memories are the largest and densest blocks of a modern chip — and the place where most manufacturing defects land. They are also tested in a completely different way from logic. This topic explains why.
objectives: Explain why embedded memories dominate chip area and defects.
Name the main memory types and what makes each one special for test.
Explain why scan, ATPG and random LBIST patterns do not test memories well, and what a memory test must do instead.

blocks.md: You met this picture in *BIST Foundations*. Look at it again with one question: **how much of the chip is memory?**

blocks.hint: Click the blocks — every yellow area is memory.
blocks.caption: A system on chip: memories in yellow

spots.title: Inside the cores
spots.md: Each core has L1 instruction and data caches, register files and small buffers — several memory instances per core.

spots.title: L2 cache
spots.md: One of the biggest blocks on the die: millions of bits, often split into many banks.

spots.title: Accelerators
spots.md: GPUs and AI engines carry large local SRAMs next to their arithmetic units.

spots.title: Hundreds of small memories
spots.md: FIFOs and buffers in every interface. Each is small, but a big SoC can contain **thousands** of memory instances — and every one must be tested.

spots.title: ROM
spots.md: Fixed boot code. It can only be read, so its test is different.

spots.title: Shared SRAM
spots.md: On-chip working memory used by all cores.

blocks.md: In many modern SoCs embedded memories take **half of the die area or more**, and they contain most of the transistors. Memory cells are drawn with the **tightest layout rules** the factory allows — smaller and denser than any logic. Dense structures catch more particles and suffer more from process variation.

blocks.title: Where the defects are
blocks.md: More area, more transistors and denser layout mean that a **large share of all manufacturing defects lands in the memories**. Chip yield is often decided by memory yield — which is why memories get their own tests, their own BIST, and even spare rows and columns for **repair**.
Not all memories are alike. Each type stores a bit in a different way — and the way a bit is stored decides how it can fail.

tabs.label: SRAM
tabs.md: **Static RAM.** Each bit is held by two cross-coupled inverters (6 transistors). Fast, keeps its value as long as power is on, no refresh. The workhorse of embedded memory: caches, buffers, FPGA block RAM. **This course focuses on SRAM.**

tabs.label: Register file
tabs.md: Small, very fast memory inside a processor, usually with **several ports** (e.g. two reads and one write per clock). Built from SRAM-like cells or flip-flops. Extra ports bring extra fault types between ports.

tabs.label: ROM
tabs.md: **Read-only memory.** Content is fixed when the chip is made (boot code, tables). It cannot be written, so it is tested by **reading every word** and compacting the data into a signature (a MISR — Topic 5 of *BIST Foundations*).

tabs.label: DRAM
tabs.md: **Dynamic RAM.** One transistor and one capacitor per bit — very dense, but the charge leaks, so every cell must be **refreshed** regularly. Usually a separate chip; its tests stress **retention** (how long a cell keeps its charge).

tabs.label: Flash / NVM
tabs.md: **Non-volatile** memory: keeps data without power (floating gate or charge trap). Found as embedded flash in microcontrollers. Slow to write, wears out after many writes; tested with special program/erase sequences.

blocks.prompt: Practice: does the memory keep its data when the power is switched off?

subsections.title: Why logic tests do not fit memories

blocks.md: Logic is tested with **scan** and **ATPG** (automatic test pattern generation) or with **LBIST**: load a pattern into the flip-flops, clock once, compare the outputs. This does not work well for memories:

items.title: Memory cells are not scan flip-flops
items.md: Scan works by chaining **flip-flops** into shift registers. The millions of cells of an SRAM are not flip-flops and cannot be chained — you can only reach them through the memory's own ports, one address at a time.

items.title: ATPG does not model the inside of a memory
items.md: ATPG tools reason about gates. A memory is a huge, analog-ish array; in ATPG it is usually treated as a **black box**. The logic around it is tested, the cells inside are not.

items.title: Memory faults depend on the order of operations
items.md: Many memory faults appear only after a **sequence**: write 0, write 1 to a *neighbour*, then read — or only when the address goes **up** rather than down. A logic pattern is a single snapshot; random patterns would almost never create the right sequence at the right address.

items.title: Every address must be visited
items.md: A defect can sit in any one of millions of cells. A memory test must write and read **every** address, several times, with known data. Random patterns would need far too long to cover all of them.

blocks.caption: A memory test: write all addresses in one order, then read and rewrite them in the other

blocks.md: Memory tests are therefore **algorithms**: fixed sequences of writes and reads that sweep through all addresses in a defined order — the **March tests** of the next training. They are regular and simple, so they are easy to put into hardware: an **address counter**, a **data generator** and a **comparator** are enough. That is **memory BIST**.

blocks.title: How we continue
blocks.md: To design good memory tests, we first need to know **how a memory works** (Topics 2–3) and **how it can fail** (Topics 4–7).

questions.text: Why does a large share of manufacturing defects land in the embedded memories?
options: Memories take much of the die area and use the densest layout, so they catch more defects.
Memories are made in a different factory.
Memory cells are larger than logic gates.
Memories are tested less often, so defects collect there.

questions.text: Which memory type holds each bit with two cross-coupled inverters and needs no refresh?
options: SRAM
DRAM
ROM
Flash

questions.text: Which memory loses its data even with power on unless it is refreshed?
options: DRAM
SRAM
ROM
Flash

questions.text: Sort the memories: does the data survive a power-off?
Why are scan, ATPG and random patterns not enough for memories? Select **all** correct answers.
options: Memory cells cannot be chained into scan shift registers.
Many memory faults appear only after a specific sequence of writes and reads.
Every one of millions of addresses must be visited.
Memories cannot have stuck-at faults.

questions.text: Which hardware does a simple memory BIST need to run a March-type test?
options: An address counter, a data generator and a comparator.
A scan chain through every memory cell.
An ATPG tool on the chip.
A second copy of the memory.
